docs.title: Home
docs.text:
Optimizing Compiler C99 Backend Flex & Bison 3AC Quadruples Computer Vision OPEX

Optimized Processing Engine for eXecution. A statically-typed domain-specific compiled language bridging algorithmic computing with first-class computer vision tensors, spatial convolution, and bare-metal native execution.

Documentation → Compiler Architecture GitHub Repository →

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
Computer Vision Primitives

First-class language types for IMAGE, MATRIX, KERNEL, and PIXEL. Direct memory layout and pixel channel manipulation without external library wrappers.

IMAGE / MATRIX / KERNEL Convolution and Pipeline Operators

2D spatial convolution via infix ** and functional stream processing via |>. Enables concise chaining such as img |> GRAYSCALE |> THRESHOLD(50).

** and |> Operators Scoped Semantic Type Checker

Hierarchical symbol table with lexical scoping, variable shadowing rules, undeclared identifier validation, and strict parameter type checking before lowering.

src/semantic.c Three-Address Code Intermediate Representation

Deterministic intermediate code represented as quadruples ([OP, ARG1, ARG2, RES]) with temporary register allocation and structured control flow labeling.

src/ir.c (Quadruples) Native C99 Code Generator

Lowers the abstract syntax tree into clean, self-contained C99 code, compiling directly to standalone Mach-O and ELF native executable binaries.

Clang / GCC Backend Unified Command-Line Driver

Single binary supporting immediate on-the-fly execution (--run), binary compilation (-o <bin>), semantic verification (--check), and grammar derivation dumps.

./opex CLI

docs.title: Language Specification
docs.text:
The following example demonstrates an end-to-end edge detection pipeline written in OPEX:

OPEX SourceThree-Address Intermediate CodeNative Execution 
PROGRAM EdgeDetectionPipeline
BEGIN
    // 1. Declare 3x3 Sobel spatial kernels
    KERNEL sobelX := [[-1, 0, 1], [-2, 0, 2], [-1, 0, 1]]
    KERNEL sobelY := [[-1, -2, -1], [ 0,  0,  0], [ 1,  2,  1]]

    // 2. Load test image & convert to grayscale
    AUTO img   := LOAD("input.jpg")
    AUTO gray  := GRAYSCALE(img)

    // 3. Convolve with Sobel filters and chain through thresholding
    AUTO edges := ((gray ** sobelX) + (gray ** sobelY)) |> THRESHOLD(50)

    // 4. Export result
    SAVE(edges, "edges.ppm")
    PRINT "Processed {img.width}x{img.height} image successfully."
END

=== THREE-ADDRESS CODE QUADRUPLES ===
[0001] PARAM       "input.jpg"             -                  -
[0002] CALL        LOAD                    1                  t1
[0003] ASSIGN      t1                      -                  img
[0004] PARAM       img                     -                  -
[0005] CALL        GRAYSCALE               1                  t2
[0006] ASSIGN      t2                      -                  gray
[0007] CONV2D      gray                    sobelX             t3
[0008] CONV2D      gray                    sobelY             t4
[0009] ADD         t3                      t4                 t5
[0010] PARAM       50                      -                  -
[0011] PIPE        t5                      THRESHOLD          t6
[0012] ASSIGN      t6                      -                  edges

$ ./opex --run tests/edge_detection.opx
Generating synthetic 64x64 sample image...
Image generated: 64x64 pixels.
Converting to grayscale...
Applying Sobel-X and Sobel-Y convolution...
Applying binary threshold filter (threshold = 60)...
Saving edge map to 'edges.ppm'...
Saved 'edges.ppm' successfully!
Generated image viewer script: view_edges.py
Run: python3 view_edges.py to inspect the output.

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text:
Build from SourceRun Test Suites 
# Clone repository
git clone https://github.com/gaurav-budhwani/OPEX.git
cd OPEX

# Build compiler binary
make

# Run any OPEX program directly
./opex --run tests/bubble_sort.opx

# Compile to a native binary
./opex -o bubble_sort tests/bubble_sort.opx
./bubble_sort

# Validate all 16 language grammar test cases
make test_all

# Execute interactive benchmark programs

docs.title: Native Code Generation
docs.text: The final compiler pass lowers the AST into standard ISO C99, linking against the OPEX runtime to generate native machine binaries.

docs.title: Why Lower to C99?
docs.text:
Rather than emitting raw assembly for a single architecture (e.g. x86-64 only), lowering through C99 provides distinct engineering advantages:

  1. Cross-Platform Portability: Compiles identically on macOS (ARM64 Apple Silicon), Linux (x86-64, AArch64), and BSD.
  2. Industrial Optimization: The host compiler (clang or gcc) automatically performs SIMD vectorization, register allocation, and dead code elimination with -O2.
  3. Robust Runtime Integration: Memory allocation, call stacks, and recursion are managed with zero overhead.

docs.title: Driver Workflow (opex --run & -o)
docs.text:
When compiling or running an OPEX program:

[OPEX Source]
     │
     ▼ (parse & validate)
[Verified AST]
     │
     ▼ (codegen.c)
[/tmp/opex_<pid>.c]  ───> Links with [src/runtime.h]
     │
     ▼ (gcc -O2 -lm)
[Native Mach-O / ELF Binary]
     │
     ▼ (execute & cleanup)
[stdout / Return Code]

docs.title: Intermediate Representation (3AC)
docs.text: Before target code generation, the compiler translates high-level AST trees into Three-Address Code (3AC) Quadruples.

docs.title: Quadruple Structure
docs.text:
Each quadruple represents a linearized instruction of the form:

\[\text{op} \quad \text{arg1} \quad \text{arg2} \quad \text{result}\] 
typedef struct Quad {
    char* op;
    char* arg1;
    char* arg2;
    char* result;
    struct Quad* next;
} Quad;

docs.title: Example: Recursive Fibonacci IR
docs.text:
For the OPEX source: 

IF n <= 1 THEN
    RETURN n;
ELSE
    RETURN fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2);
ENDIF

The SDT engine emits the following quadruples:

op           arg1            arg2            result         
-----------------------------------------------------------
func         fib                                            
<=           n               1               t1             
ifFalse      t1                              L2             
return       n                                              
goto                                         L1             
Label                                        L2             
-            n               1               t2             
param        t2                                             
call         fib             1               t3             
-            n               2               t4             
param        t4                                             
call         fib             1               t5             
+            t3              t5              t6             
return       t6                                             
Label                                        L1             
endfunc      fib

docs.title: Control Flow Flattening
docs.text:
• Conditionals (IF / ELSE): Flattens nested blocks using conditional ifFalse <cond> <label> jumps.
  • Loops (WHILE, FOR): Injects a top loop marker (L_start), evaluates the invariant, and jumps back upon iteration completion (goto L_start).
  • Temporary Register Management: Dynamically allocates unbounded virtual registers (t1, t2, t3, ...).

docs.title: Lexical Analysis (Flex)
docs.text: The Lexical Analyzer is the first phase of the OPEX compiler. It transforms an unformatted stream of source characters into a structured sequence of atomic tokens.

docs.title: Token Classifications
docs.text:
Tokens in OPEX are categorized into distinct semantic groups:

Category Sample Tokens Regex Pattern Keywords PROGRAM, FUNCTION, STRUCT, VAR, AUTO Direct string match CV Keywords IMAGE, MATRIX, KERNEL, PIXEL Direct string match Operators :=, **, |>, +, -, *, /, ==, != Exact operator match Separators [, ], (, ), :, ;, ,, . Single-character punctuation Identifiers myVar, sobelX, _temp ([a-zA-Z]|_)([a-zA-Z0-9]|_)* Integer Literals 0, 42, 100 [0-9]+ Float Literals 3.14, 0.001 [0-9]+\.[0-9]+([eE][+-]?[0-9]+)? String Literals "Hello {name}" \"([^\"\\\n]\|\\.)*\"

docs.title: Column & Coordinate Tracking
docs.text:
To enable precise compiler diagnostic reporting, the lexer intercepts token consumption via Flex's YY_USER_ACTION macro:

int yycolumn = 1;

#define YY_USER_ACTION \
    yylloc.first_line = yylineno; \
    yylloc.last_line = yylineno; \
    yylloc.first_column = yycolumn; \
    yylloc.last_column = yycolumn + yyleng - 1; \
    yycolumn += yyleng;

When a newline \n is encountered, yycolumn resets to 1, while yylineno increments automatically.

docs.title: Syntax & LALR(1) Parsing
docs.text: The Syntax Analyzer enforces the formal Context-Free Grammar (CFG) of OPEX using GNU Bison (Yacc) to construct an LALR(1) finite state automaton.

docs.title: Conflict Resolution: 172 to 0 Fatal Conflicts
docs.text: Initial grammar specifications frequently exhibit structural overlaps. In our preliminary Bison build, the automaton contained: - 81 Shift/Reduce Conflicts: Stemming from optional semicolons (OptSemi) and operator precedence lookaheads. - 173 Reduce/Reduce Conflicts: Fatal intersections where multiple non-terminals overlapped on identical token sequences (notably in State 74, where standalone function calls overlapped with general expressions).

docs.title: Resolution Strategy
docs.text:
1. Collapsed Expression Wrappers: Stripped duplicated expression layers (Statement -> Expr vs Statement -> FuncCallStmt).
  2. Normalized Array Definitions: Replaced specialized integer-only dimensions with generalized expressions.
  3. Formal Operator Precedence: Assigned explicit Bison %left and %right precedence declarations.

Result: Reduced the 173 Reduce/Reduce conflicts down to precisely 0 fatal conflicts (1 harmless structural lookahead in State 57 for user-defined struct types).

docs.title: Reverse Derivation Tree
docs.text:
A Bottom-Up LALR(1) parser naturally uncovers Rightmost derivations in reverse order.

During parsing, semantic actions allocate tree nodes (make_node()):

Program:
    TOK_PROGRAM TOK_ID Declarations MainBlock { 
        $$ = make_node("Program", NULL, 4, $1, $2, $3, $4); 
        root = $$; 
    }

Running ./opex --derivations < file.opx traverses the resulting AST in post-order, printing the exact derivation sequence used by the shift-reduce stack.

docs.title: Automated Parsing Table Extraction
docs.text:
Using print_table.py, Bison's raw diagnostic output (parser.output) is processed into an Excel-compatible CSV parsing table:

python3 print_table.py > table.csv

The resulting table maps all 339 states against every terminal and non-terminal symbol with their associated shift, reduce, and goto transitions.

docs.title: Compiler Architecture & Pipeline
docs.text: The OPEX compiler is built using a classical multi-pass architecture, engineered for correctness, clean abstractions, and native machine execution.

docs.title: High-Level Compilation Flow
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    subgraph FrontEnd ["Front-End Phase"]
        Src["Source Code (.opx)"] --> Lexer["Lexical Analyzer (Flex)"]
        Lexer --> Tokens["Token Stream"]
        Tokens --> Parser["Syntax Analyzer (Bison)"]
        Parser --> AST["Abstract Syntax Tree (AST)"]
    end

    subgraph MiddleEnd ["Middle-End Phase"]
        AST --> Semantic["Semantic Analyzer & Symbol Table"]
        Semantic -->|"Phase 1: IR Generation"| SDT["Syntax Directed Translation"]
        SDT --> IR["Three-Address Code (3AC Quadruples)"]
    end

    subgraph BackEnd ["Back-End Phase"]
        Semantic -->|"Phase 2: Code Generation"| Lowering["C99 Low-Level Code Generator"]
        Lowering --> CSource["Intermediate C Source (.c)"]
        CSource --> Runtime["OPEX Runtime (runtime.h)"]
        Runtime --> HostCC["Host C Compiler (GCC / Clang)"]
        HostCC --> Binary["Native Machine Binary (Mach-O / ELF)"]
    end

    classDef stage fill:#ffffff,stroke:#2563eb,stroke-width:1.5px,color:#0f172a,rx:6px,ry:6px;
    classDef sub fill:#f8fafc,stroke:#cbd5e1,stroke-width:1px,color:#1e293b;

    class FrontEnd,MiddleEnd,BackEnd sub;

docs.title: 1. Front-End: Lexing & Parsing
docs.text:
• Scanner: Implemented in Flex (src/lexer.l). Recognizes keywords, literals, range operators, and comments. Automatically tracks column and line coordinates via YY_USER_ACTION.
  • Parser: Implemented in Bison (src/parser.y). Validates syntax against an LALR(1) Context-Free Grammar.
  • AST Construction: Semantic actions dynamically allocate memory for an N-ary Abstract Syntax Tree (src/ast.c).

docs.title: 2. Middle-End: Semantic Validation & 3AC
docs.text:
• Semantic Analyzer: Traverses the AST with a scoped symbol table to catch undeclared variables and duplicate declarations (src/semantic.c).
  • Intermediate Representation: Post-order AST traversal emits Three-Address Code (3AC) Quadruples (op, arg1, arg2, result) managing temporary registers and jump labels (src/ir.c).

docs.title: 3. Back-End: Native Code Generation
docs.text:
• Target Lowering: Lowers the verified AST into clean, structured C99 (src/codegen.c).
  • Runtime Library: Links against a self-contained header (src/runtime.h) implementing memory buffers, convolution, and image filtering.
  • Native Execution: Invokes gcc/clang to generate bare-metal executables.

docs.title: Built-in Computer Vision Operations
docs.text: OPEX includes a set of native built-in operations for image processing and transformation.

docs.title: LOAD(path : STRING) : IMAGE
docs.text:
Loads an image file into memory. If the file is not found, the OPEX runtime automatically synthesizes a geometric test gradient to allow algorithm verification without local assets.

AUTO img := LOAD("landscape.ppm")

docs.title: SAVE(img : IMAGE, path : STRING) : VOID
docs.text:
Writes the image buffer to disk in standard PPM/BMP format.

SAVE(img, "output.ppm")

docs.title: GRAYSCALE(img : IMAGE) : IMAGE
docs.text:
Converts a 3-channel RGB image into a single-channel luminance intensity map using ITU-R BT.601 coefficients:

\[Y = 0.299R + 0.587G + 0.114B\] 
AUTO gray := GRAYSCALE(img)

docs.title: THRESHOLD(img : IMAGE, cutoff : INT) : IMAGE
docs.text:
Performs binary segmentation. Pixels with intensity \(\ge \text{cutoff}\) are mapped to 255 (white); otherwise 0 (black).

AUTO binaryMask := THRESHOLD(gray, 128)

docs.title: BLUR(img : IMAGE) : IMAGE
docs.text:
Applies a normalized \(3 \times 3\) box-filter spatial smoothing kernel.

AUTO smoothed := BLUR(img)

docs.title: ROTATE(img : IMAGE, degrees : INT) : IMAGE
docs.text:
Rotates the image clockwise by 90-degree increments, swapping row and column dimensions.

AUTO rotated := ROTATE(img, 90)

docs.title: FLIP(img : IMAGE, mode : INT) : IMAGE
docs.text:
Flips the image along an axis (mode = 0 for horizontal reflection, mode = 1 for vertical).

AUTO mirrored := FLIP(img, 0)

docs.title: Computer Vision Types
docs.text: A core innovation in OPEX is its native, first-class support for computer vision data structures.

docs.title: 1. IMAGE
docs.text: Represents a 2D multi-channel or single-channel image. An IMAGE carries width, height, and channel metadata alongside its underlying pixel buffer.

docs.title: Declaration & Dimensions
docs.text:
// Uninitialized image variable (loaded via LOAD)
VAR img : IMAGE;

// Direct property access
PRINT "Width:    {img.width}";
PRINT "Height:   {img.height}";
PRINT "Channels: {img.channels}";

docs.title: 2. KERNEL
docs.text: A KERNEL is a 2D spatial convolution matrix. Kernels typically have odd dimensions (e.g. 3x3, 5x5) so they possess a unique center origin.

docs.title: Kernel Literals
docs.text:
// 3x3 Sobel Horizontal Derivative Kernel
KERNEL sobelX := [[-1, 0, 1],
                  [-2, 0, 2],
                  [-1, 0, 1]]

// 3x3 Sobel Vertical Derivative Kernel
KERNEL sobelY := [[-1, -2, -1],
                  [ 0,  0,  0],
                  [ 1,  2,  1]]

// 3x3 Box Blur Kernel
KERNEL blurKernel := [[1, 1, 1],
                      [1, 1, 1],
                      [1, 1, 1]]

docs.title: 3. MATRIX
docs.text:
Represents a general 2D floating-point matrix for linear transformations, affine mappings, and coordinate projections.

VAR transform : MATRIX;

docs.title: 4. PIXEL
docs.text:
Represents a single multi-channel color or intensity value:

Field Type Meaning .r INT Red channel (0–255) .g INT Green channel (0–255) .b INT Blue channel (0–255) .v INT Grayscale intensity value 
VAR px : PIXEL;
px.r := 255;
px.g := 128;
px.b := 0;

docs.title: Convolution & Pipeline Operators
docs.text: OPEX introduces dedicated syntax operators for computer vision workflows.

docs.title: The 2D Convolution Operator (**)
docs.text:
The infix ** operator performs 2D spatial convolution between an IMAGE (or MATRIX) and a KERNEL:

\[\text{Output}(x, y) = \sum_{i=-k}^{k} \sum_{j=-k}^{k} \text{Input}(x+i, y+j) \cdot \text{Kernel}(i, j)\] 
KERNEL sobelX := [[-1, 0, 1], [-2, 0, 2], [-1, 0, 1]]
AUTO img := LOAD("sample.jpg")
AUTO gray := GRAYSCALE(img)

// Compute horizontal gradient map via convolution
AUTO edgesX := gray ** sobelX

docs.title: Edge Handling
docs.text: The OPEX runtime automatically clamps pixel boundaries with zero-padding to prevent memory overflow at image borders.

docs.title: The Pipeline Operator (|>)
docs.text:
Inspired by modern functional languages, the |> pipeline operator feeds the output of the left-hand expression as the first argument into the right-hand function call:

// Traditional nested syntax:
AUTO result := THRESHOLD(GRAYSCALE(LOAD("input.jpg")), 50)

// Equivalent clean OPEX pipeline syntax:
AUTO result := LOAD("input.jpg") 
               |> GRAYSCALE 
               |> THRESHOLD(50)

docs.title: Combined Pipeline Example
docs.text: AUTO edgeMap := ((gray ** sobelX) + (gray ** sobelY)) |> THRESHOLD(50)

docs.title: Data Structures
docs.text: Implementations of classical computer science data structures using OPEX STRUCT compositions and functions.

docs.title: 1. Struct-Based Stack (tests/stack.opx)
docs.text:
PROGRAM StackDemo
    STRUCT Stack
        data : ARRAY[10] OF INT;
        top : INT;
    ENDSTRUCT

    VAR s : Stack;

    FUNCTION push(val : INT) : VOID
    BEGIN
        IF s.top >= 9 THEN
            PRINT "Error: Stack Overflow";
        ELSE
            s.top := s.top + 1;
            s.data[s.top] := val;
        ENDIF
    END

    FUNCTION pop() : INT
    BEGIN
        VAR val : INT;
        IF s.top < 0 THEN
            PRINT "Error: Stack Underflow";
            RETURN -1;
        ELSE
            val := s.data[s.top];
            s.top := s.top - 1;
            RETURN val;
        ENDIF
    END

MAIN
BEGIN
    s.top := -1;

    PRINT "Pushing 10, 20, 30...";
    push(10);
    push(20);
    push(30);

    PRINT "Popping values...";
    PRINT pop(); // 30
    PRINT pop(); // 20
    PRINT pop(); // 10
END

docs.title: 2. Circular Queue (tests/queue.opx)
docs.text:
PROGRAM QueueDemo
    STRUCT Queue
        data : ARRAY[5] OF INT;
        head : INT;
        tail : INT;
        count : INT;
        capacity : INT;
    ENDSTRUCT

    VAR q : Queue;

    FUNCTION enqueue(val : INT) : VOID
    BEGIN
        IF q.count == q.capacity THEN
            PRINT "Error: Queue Full";
        ELSE
            q.data[q.tail] := val;
            q.tail := (q.tail + 1) % q.capacity;
            q.count := q.count + 1;
        ENDIF
    END

    FUNCTION dequeue() : INT
    BEGIN
        VAR val : INT;
        IF q.count == 0 THEN
            PRINT "Error: Queue Empty";
            RETURN -1;
        ELSE
            val := q.data[q.head];
            q.head := (q.head + 1) % q.capacity;
            q.count := q.count - 1;
            RETURN val;
        ENDIF
    END

MAIN
BEGIN
    q.head := 0;
    q.tail := 0;
    q.count := 0;
    q.capacity := 5;

    PRINT "Enqueueing 1, 2, 3...";
    enqueue(1);
    enqueue(2);
    enqueue(3);

    PRINT "Dequeueing...";
    PRINT dequeue(); // 1
    PRINT dequeue(); // 2
END

docs.title: Edge Detection Pipeline
docs.text: This example demonstrates the complete computer vision capability of OPEX by computing horizontal and vertical image gradients using Sobel operators, combining them, and applying threshold segmentation.

docs.title: OPEX Source (tests/edge_detection.opx)
docs.text:
PROGRAM EdgeDetection
BEGIN
    // Define 3x3 Sobel spatial kernels
    KERNEL sobelX := [[-1, 0, 1],
                      [-2, 0, 2],
                      [-1, 0, 1]]

    KERNEL sobelY := [[-1, -2, -1],
                      [ 0,  0,  0],
                      [ 1,  2,  1]]

    // Load and convert to grayscale
    AUTO img  := LOAD("input.jpg")
    AUTO gray := GRAYSCALE(img)

    // Apply Sobel convolution operators
    AUTO edgesX := gray ** sobelX
    AUTO edgesY := gray ** sobelY

    // Combine gradient maps (element-wise addition)
    AUTO combined := edgesX + edgesY

    // Threshold via pipeline operator to produce binary edge map
    AUTO edgeMap := combined |> THRESHOLD(50)

    // Save output and print metadata
    SAVE(edgeMap, "edges.png")
    PRINT "Edge detection complete: {img.width}x{img.height}"
END

docs.title: Recursive Algorithms
docs.text: OPEX fully supports recursive subroutines with stack frame management.

docs.title: 1. Recursive Fibonacci (tests/fibonacci.opx)
docs.text:
PROGRAM FibRecursive
    FUNCTION fib(n : INT) : INT
    BEGIN
        IF n <= 1 THEN
            RETURN n;
        ELSE
            RETURN fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2);
        ENDIF
    END

MAIN
BEGIN
    VAR terms : INT;
    VAR i : INT;

    PRINT "How many terms?";
    INPUT terms;

    PRINT "Fibonacci Sequence:";
    FOR i := 0 TO terms DO
        PRINT fib(i);
    ENDFOR
END

docs.title: 2. Recursive Euclidean GCD (tests/gcd_recursive.opx)
docs.text:
PROGRAM GCDRecursive
    FUNCTION gcd(a : INT, b : INT) : INT
    BEGIN
        IF b == 0 THEN
            RETURN a;
        ELSE
            RETURN gcd(b, a % b);
        ENDIF
    END

MAIN
BEGIN
    VAR num1 : INT;
    VAR num2 : INT;
    VAR result : INT;

    PRINT "Enter first number:";
    INPUT num1;
    PRINT "Enter second number:";
    INPUT num2;

    result := gcd(num1, num2);
    PRINT "GCD of {num1} and {num2} is {result}";
END

docs.title: Sorting & Searching
docs.text: Algorithmic implementations in OPEX demonstrating array manipulations, nested loops, and binary search.

docs.title: 1. Bubble Sort (tests/bubble_sort.opx)
docs.text:
Sorts an array of 5 integers in ascending order:

PROGRAM BubbleSort
BEGIN
    VAR arr : ARRAY[5] OF INT;
    VAR i : INT;
    VAR j : INT;
    VAR temp : INT;
    VAR n : INT;

    n := 5;

    // Initialize unsorted array
    arr[0] := 64;
    arr[1] := 34;
    arr[2] := 25;
    arr[3] := 12;
    arr[4] := 22;

    PRINT "Sorting array...";

    // Bubble Sort nested loops
    FOR i := 0 TO n - 2 DO
        FOR j := 0 TO n - i - 2 DO
            IF arr[j] > arr[j + 1] THEN
                temp := arr[j];
                arr[j] := arr[j + 1];
                arr[j + 1] := temp;
            ENDIF
        ENDFOR
    ENDFOR

    PRINT "Sorted Array:";
    FOREACH val IN arr DO
        PRINT val;
    ENDFOR
END

docs.title: 2. Binary Search (tests/binary_search.opx)
docs.text:
Performs \(O(\log n)\) logarithmic search over a sorted 10-element array:

PROGRAM BinarySearch
BEGIN
    VAR data : ARRAY[10] OF INT;
    VAR target : INT;
    VAR low : INT;
    VAR high : INT;
    VAR mid : INT;
    VAR found : BOOL;

    FOR low := 0 TO 9 DO
        data[low] := low * 2;
    ENDFOR

    PRINT "Enter value to search for:";
    INPUT target;

    low := 0;
    high := 9;
    found := FALSE;

    WHILE low <= high DO
        mid := (low + high) / 2;
        IF data[mid] == target THEN
            PRINT "Found at index: {mid}";
            found := TRUE;
            low := high + 1; // Break
        ELSE
            IF data[mid] < target THEN
                low := mid + 1;
            ELSE
                high := mid - 1;
            ENDIF
        ENDIF
    ENDWHILE

    IF found == FALSE THEN
        PRINT "Value not found";
    ENDIF
END

docs.title: Hello World in OPEX
docs.text: Every OPEX source file uses the .opx extension and follows a clear program structure.

docs.title: Your First Program
docs.text:
Create a file named hello.opx:

PROGRAM HelloWorld
BEGIN
    PRINT "Hello, OPEX World!";

    VAR year : INT;
    year := 2026;

    PRINT "Compiler running in year {year}!";
END

docs.title: Running Your Program
docs.text: You have two primary ways to run an OPEX program:

docs.title: Method 1: On-the-Fly Execution (--run)
docs.text:
Executes the code directly, ideal for quick testing, development, and scripting:

./opex --run hello.opx

Output: 

Hello, OPEX World!
Compiler running in year 2026!

docs.title: Method 2: Standalone Native Binary Compilation (-o)
docs.text:
Compiles the OPEX code into an optimized native machine binary (Mach-O on macOS, ELF on Linux):

# Compile to a native executable
./opex -o hello hello.opx

# Inspect the binary
file hello
# Output: hello: Mach-O 64-bit executable arm64

# Execute anywhere
./hello

docs.title: Program Structure Anatomy
docs.text:
1. PROGRAM <Identifier>: Defines the program entry namespace.
  2. BEGIN ... END or MAIN BEGIN ... END: Encloses the main executable block.
  3. VAR <Identifier> : <Type>;: Statically typed variable declaration.
  4. :=: The OPEX assignment operator.
  5. PRINT "<text> {variable}": Formatted output with dynamic string interpolation.

docs.title: Installation & Setup
docs.text: Get started with the OPEX language and compiler in minutes.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
OPEX requires standard C build tools available on macOS and Linux systems:

Dependency Minimum Version Description GCC or Clang C99 compliant Host C compiler used for building the compiler and lowering code Flex 2.6+ Fast Lexical Analyzer Generator Bison (Yacc) 3.8+ LALR(1) Parser Generator Make GNU Make 3.81+ Automation tool macOS (Homebrew)Ubuntu / DebianArch Linux 
brew install flex bison make
# Ensure Homebrew bison/flex are in your PATH if using Apple Silicon
export PATH="/opt/homebrew/opt/bison/bin:$PATH"
export PATH="/opt/homebrew/opt/flex/bin:$PATH"

sudo apt update
sudo apt install -y build-essential flex bison

sudo pacman -S base-devel flex bison

docs.title: Build from Source
docs.text:
# Clone the repository
git clone https://github.com/gaurav-budhwani/OPEX.git
cd OPEX

# Compile the compiler binary
make

This compiles both ./parser and creates the ./opex CLI driver in the root directory.

docs.title: System-Wide Installation (Optional)
docs.text:
To invoke opex globally from any directory on your computer:

sudo make install

Now you can run:

opex --run program.opx

docs.title: Verifying the Installation
docs.text:
Run the built-in test suite to ensure the front-end, semantic analyzer, and native code generator are working properly:

# Run syntax and parsing checks
make test_all

# Run semantic validation
make test_semantic

# Run live algorithmic and computer vision test cases
make test_run

docs.title: Control Flow
docs.text: OPEX provides modern, expressive constructs for branching and looping.

docs.title: Conditionals (IF ... THEN ... ELSE)
docs.text:
Conditionals evaluate boolean expressions:

IF score >= 90 THEN
    PRINT "Grade: A";
ELSE
    IF score >= 75 THEN
        PRINT "Grade: B";
    ELSE
        PRINT "Grade: C";
    ENDIF
ENDIF

docs.title: Count-Controlled Loop (FOR)
docs.text:
The FOR loop iterates an integer variable from a start expression to an end expression inclusive:

// Basic loop from 0 to 9 (step = 1)
FOR i := 0 TO 9 DO
    PRINT i;
ENDFOR

// Loop with custom STEP increment
FOR i := 0 TO 100 STEP 10 DO
    PRINT i;
ENDFOR

docs.title: Collection Traversal (FOREACH IN)
docs.text:
Iterate over array elements without manual index management:

VAR numbers : ARRAY[5] OF INT;
// Fill numbers...

FOREACH val IN numbers DO
    PRINT val;
ENDFOR

docs.title: Condition-Controlled Loop (WHILE)
docs.text:
Executes statements while the condition evaluates to TRUE:

VAR count : INT;
count := 10;

WHILE count > 0 DO
    PRINT count;
    count := count - 1;
ENDWHILE

docs.title: Pattern Matching (MATCH ... WHEN)
docs.text:
The MATCH statement replaces nested if-else chains with clean pattern branches:

MATCH status
    WHEN 200:
        PRINT "HTTP OK";
    WHEN 404:
        PRINT "HTTP Not Found";
    WHEN 500:
        PRINT "Server Error";
ENDMATCH

docs.title: Functions & Structs
docs.text: OPEX supports modular program architecture through functions, recursion, and user-defined product types (STRUCT).

docs.title: Functions
docs.text:
Functions are defined with explicit parameter lists and return types:

FUNCTION add(a : INT, b : INT) : INT
BEGIN
    RETURN a + b;
END

FUNCTION logMessage(msg : STRING) : VOID
BEGIN
    PRINT msg;
END

docs.title: Recursive Functions
docs.text:
OPEX features full support for deep recursion with native call-stack frame management:

// Recursive Fibonacci
FUNCTION fib(n : INT) : INT
BEGIN
    IF n <= 1 THEN
        RETURN n;
    ELSE
        RETURN fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2);
    ENDIF
END

// Recursive Greatest Common Divisor (GCD)
FUNCTION gcd(a : INT, b : INT) : INT
BEGIN
    IF b == 0 THEN
        RETURN a;
    ELSE
        RETURN gcd(b, a % b);
    ENDIF
END

docs.title: User-Defined Structs (STRUCT)
docs.text:
STRUCT definitions group related data into custom record types:

STRUCT Point
    x : INT;
    y : INT;
ENDSTRUCT

STRUCT Stack
    data : ARRAY[10] OF INT;
    top : INT;
ENDSTRUCT

docs.title: Struct Instantiation and Field Access
docs.text:
Struct members are accessed using the dot (.) operator:

VAR s : Stack;

// Initialize stack fields
s.top := -1;
s.top := s.top + 1;
s.data[s.top] := 100;

PRINT "Top index: {s.top}";
PRINT "Top value: {s.data[s.top]}";

docs.title: Input & Output
docs.text: OPEX provides clean, high-level primitives for standard I/O and dynamic string interpolation.

docs.title: Output (PRINT)
docs.text: The PRINT statement outputs values to standard output (stdout), automatically appending a newline.

docs.title: Basic Printing
docs.text:
PRINT "Hello World";
PRINT 42;
PRINT 3.14159;
PRINT TRUE;

docs.title: String Interpolation
docs.text:
String literals can embed any variable or property expression inside {...} braces:

VAR name : STRING;
VAR score : INT;

name := "Alice";
score := 98;

PRINT "Player {name} achieved a score of {score}!";

Interpolation also supports accessing struct fields and image metadata:

PRINT "Image resolution: {img.width}x{img.height}";
PRINT "Current node: {node.id}, distance: {node.dist}";

docs.title: Input (INPUT)
docs.text:
The INPUT statement reads values from standard input (stdin) into a target variable:

VAR age : INT;
PRINT "Enter your age:";
INPUT age;

PRINT "You will be {age + 1} next year.";

docs.title: Types & Variables
docs.text: OPEX is a statically-typed language with compile-time type checking and support for implicit type inference.

docs.title: Primitive Data Types
docs.text: Type Bit Width Description Default INT 64-bit Signed integers, pixel coordinates, loop counters 0 FLOAT 64-bit Double precision IEEE 754 floating point numbers 0.0 BOOL 8-bit Boolean flags (TRUE, FALSE) FALSE STRING Dynamic UTF-8 string literals with {var} interpolation "" VOID 0-bit Function return type indicating no return value N/A

docs.title: Explicit Declarations (VAR)
docs.text:
Variables declared using the VAR keyword must explicitly define their type:

VAR count : INT;
VAR pi : FLOAT;
VAR active : BOOL;
VAR greeting : STRING;

count := 42;
pi := 3.1415926535;
active := TRUE;
greeting := "Welcome to OPEX";

docs.title: Type Inference (AUTO)
docs.text:
The AUTO keyword deduces the variable's type from its initialization expression at compile time:

AUTO steps := 100;           // Inferred as INT
AUTO threshold := 0.75;      // Inferred as FLOAT
AUTO enabled := TRUE;        // Inferred as BOOL
AUTO label := "Normalized";  // Inferred as STRING

Note: Once inferred, the type of an AUTO variable is immutable. You cannot assign a float to an AUTO variable initialized with an integer.

docs.title: Collections (ARRAY)
docs.text: Arrays in OPEX are fixed-size, homogeneous collections allocated in contiguous memory.

docs.title: 1D Arrays
docs.text:
// 10-element integer array
VAR buffer : ARRAY[10] OF INT;

buffer[0] := 5;
buffer[1] := 10;

docs.title: 2D Arrays (Matrices)
docs.text:
// 3x3 matrix
VAR grid : ARRAY[3][3] OF INT;

grid[0][0] := 1;
grid[0][1] := 0;
grid[0][2] := 0;

docs.title: Array Slicing
docs.text:
Arrays support range-based slicing using the .. operator:

VAR subRegion : ARRAY[5][10] OF INT;
subRegion := matrixA[0..5];

docs.title: Academic Course Reports & Deliverables
docs.text: The development of the OPEX compiler was structured across 4 rigorous technical design milestones under Prof. Shouvick Mondal.

docs.title: 1. Assignment 2: Lexical Analysis
docs.text:
• Focus: Regular expressions, DFA state machines, Flex specifications, token frequency analysis.
  • Repository PDF: A2_Report.pdf
  • Key Deliverable: Implementation of src/lexer.l with coordinate tracking.

docs.title: 2. Assignment 3: Syntax Analysis
docs.text:
• Focus: Context-Free Grammars (CFG), LALR(1) state generation in Bison, Bottom-Up reverse derivation tracking, resolution of 172 Reduce/Reduce conflicts, and automated parsing table generation.
  • Repository PDF: A3_Report.pdf
  • LaTeX Source: A3_Report.tex
  • Key Deliverable: Parser implementation in src/parser.y and table generator print_table.py.

docs.title: 3. Assignment 4: Intermediate Code Generation
docs.text:
• Focus: Syntax-Directed Translation (SDT), post-order AST traversal, virtual registers (t1, t2), label jump algorithms, and Three-Address Code (3AC) Quadruple outputs.
  • Repository PDF: A4_Report.pdf
  • LaTeX Source: A4_Report.tex
  • Key Deliverable: Intermediate code generator src/ir.c and 17 generated IR quadruple logs in ir_outputs/.

docs.title: 4. Language Specification
docs.text:
• Authoritative Manual: language_specifications.pdf
  • Outlines the complete lexical rules, grammar, operator precedence tables, and computer vision typing expectations.
